reason: The text portrays multiple members of the elite unfavorably. The King of Israel is depicted as desperate, helpless, and emotionally distraught—tearing his clothes and making rash vows while the city starves. The Shalish (royal officer who 'leans on the king's hand') is shown as arrogant and mocking, sarcastically questioning the prophet Elisha's word about divine salvation. Most tellingly, he is subsequently trampled to death by the people and denied the food he doubted would come—a degrading fulfillment of the curse. In contrast, the four lepers—the common, marginalized people—are portrayed heroically as resourceful, wise, and ultimately as the saviors of the city. The foreign king Ben-Hadad is depicted as an antagonist causing suffering. The narrative structure itself privileges the lower-status figures while showing the elite as weak, foolish, or antagonistic.
